description:
Why does creation await the resurrection of God’s children? Wesam Saad answers by tracing the connection between humanity and the world God made. Beginning with Genesis, he explains that human life as body and soul was good before sin brought curse, pain and death. He reads the promised restoration of all things alongside Revelation’s removal of those consequences. In Romans 8, creation shares humanity’s bondage and also awaits its deliverance. Its groaning resembles childbirth rather than a final disappearance, supporting his expectation of renewed physical life in a restored creation. He urges listeners to let that hope shape their desires, rather than remain an interesting idea.

The discussion then turns to the lasting significance of present spiritual growth. Saad distinguishes the complete rejection of known sin from the continuing pursuit of holiness, love and joy. In his explanation, removal of sin does not make a finite creature infinitely mature. He argues that the heart’s present growth affects its future capacity to enjoy God, while affirming that growth continues in eternity. Suffering provides an opportunity for growth that will not remain in the eternal state. The practical challenge is to attend to the heart now, including responses to offence and opportunities to help others, instead of allowing spiritual laziness to become normal.

questions.question: Why does Saad begin with humanity’s creation as body and soul?
questions.answer: He is clarifying continuity between present human life and the eternal state. Genesis describes embodied humanity as part of God’s good creation, so Saad understands restoration as removing sin’s effects rather than replacing human beings with another kind of creature. The opening also revisits questions left from the preceding resurrection session.

questions.question: How does the session connect humanity’s fall with creation’s future?
questions.answer: Saad reads Romans 8 as joining creation’s condition to humanity’s condition. Creation did not itself choose Adam’s sin, but it shared the resulting corruption. Its future liberation is likewise connected to the revealing of God’s children and the redemption of their bodies.

questions.question: Why is the comparison with childbirth important to his argument?
questions.answer: Childbirth involves suffering that leads to new life, rather than simply ending in disappearance. Saad contrasts that image with the final suffering of someone dying to explain why he expects continuity and restoration for creation. He uses it to reinforce the connection between bodily resurrection and the renewal of the world.

questions.question: What difference does Saad identify between rejecting sin and pursuing holiness?
questions.answer: Known sin is to be put away completely, without negotiating for a portion of it to remain. Holiness, love and knowledge of Christ are described as things in which believers keep growing. He uses that distinction to encourage decisive resistance to sin together with an ongoing commitment to spiritual maturity.

questions.question: Why does freedom from sin not mean infinite maturity in this teaching?
questions.answer: Saad distinguishes the absence of a sinful condition from possessing a virtue without limit. The absence of misery does not, in his explanation, make a person infinitely joyful, just as the absence of pride does not imply infinite humility. God alone is infinite, while created people continue to grow.

questions.question: How does Saad connect present sanctification with future enjoyment of God?
questions.answer: He teaches that the heart’s growth in this life carries into the eternal state and affects its capacity for enjoyment. All believers will be free from pain, but he argues that their capacities will differ. His practical warning is against neglecting spiritual growth now on the assumption that glorification will make everyone equally mature.

questions.question: Does the session teach that spiritual growth stops in eternity?
questions.answer: No. Saad explicitly affirms continuing growth in the knowledge and enjoyment of Christ. He distinguishes that growth from the present opportunity to grow through suffering, which will no longer exist in the eternal state. His discussion of Ephesians connects ongoing growth with the inexhaustible love of Christ.

questions.question: Which everyday responses does the session ask listeners to examine?
questions.answer: Saad asks listeners to consider how they respond when offended and how they treat people who need their help. He warns against letting the demands and distractions of daily life become a reason to neglect the heart. The application is to pursue love, unity and spiritual growth deliberately, with their eternal significance in view.
